summary: Strait of Belle Isle light lit 15 March 1858 in a limestone tower; the historic tower has been inactive since 2017 and the active light shows from a skeletal tower.

lens.where: original first-order lens of the historic upper tower (Lighthouse Directory)

structures.note: Faced with firebrick and shingles; inactive since 2017 (Lighthouse Directory).
Short skeletal tower carrying the active light (Lighthouse Directory; Coast Guard list gives a square skeleton tower).
Attached one-and-a-half-storey stone keeper's house (Lighthouse Directory); double dwelling finished by end of 1856 (Lighthouse Friends).
New wooden fog alarm building, 1909; fog alarm moved to the upper light in 1912 (Lighthouse Friends).

events.note: François Baby contracted to build four major Gulf lights, Belle Isle among them
Keepers' double dwelling finished by end of 1856
Tower completed; workers returned in 1857 after leaving at the end of the 1856 season
Fixed white light first shown 15 March 1858 with a first-order Fresnel lens from Paris
Tower covered with clapboards against frost and easterly winds
Struck by lightning at 9:30 p.m., 9 August 1876; keeper Martin Coltin and a family member seriously injured
Second, lower light established about 91 m (300 ft) lower, in a wooden pyramidal tower with a fixed catoptric light
Rockets put into service as fog signal from 1891, after trials in 1890
First-order double sirens began operating 9 September 1899; compressed air from a water wheel at the landing
Steamer Scotsman ashore in the Strait of Belle Isle, reported 28 September 1899; Montfort reported carrying 249 survivors to Rimouski (Dakota Chief wire; another item says 250)
Wooden lower-light tower dismantled; new metal lantern with second-order lens, occulting light
New wooden fog alarm building
Fog alarm moved to the upper lighthouse
Radio direction-finding station established near the light
Lighthouse electrified; from 1958 power came from the radio station
Fire in the fog alarm building; three keepers burned and flown to hospital in St. Anthony
Upper and lower lights and keepers' duplex declared Recognized Federal Heritage Buildings
Station de-staffed; upper and lower lights remained active (Lighthouse Friends)
Heritage status granted (Lighthouse Directory)
Historic upper tower inactive since 2017; active light moved to a short skeletal tower (date of move not given)

wrecks.outcome: Dominion Line steamer from Liverpool ashore in the Strait of Belle Isle (dispatch of 28 Sept.); Montfort reported carrying 249 survivors to Rimouski, a wire said fifteen drowned, and other items gave 250 passengers; no death toll in Department reports. The Department's 1900 report, under its Cape Norman station, says the wreck's cargo floated around the vicinity.
Steamer carrying fodder for the construction horses wrecked; the island had no vegetation for them (Lighthouse Friends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources differ on whether the light is still lit. The Coast Guard's list gives the station's light as a white flash every 20 seconds (Fl W 20s) at 137.1 m (CCG). The Lighthouse Directory says the historic 1858 tower has been inactive since 2017, and that the active light has moved to a short skeletal tower. Both are consistent: the light is lit, the old tower is not.

The Lighthouse Directory gives 1858. Lighthouse Friends says the workers returned in 1857 to complete the tower and that the lens first showed on 15 March 1858. The record's 1858 is the year the light was lit, so the record stands; 1857 is recorded as the completion year.
The 2017 event in the record refers to the historic tower. The active light has continued from a skeletal tower, so the station is active.

Lighthouse Friends gives 1901 to 1906. The Department's keeper list for the year ended 30 June 1907 still names 'Colton, P. J' at Belle Isle Light and Fog Alarm, so the record's end year is taken as 1907 (approximate). Thibaudeau's start (1907 in LF) is kept as LF gives it.

notes_for_editor: Corrections made in this check: (1) the signal-flags remark in the 1900 report is under the Cape Norman station, not Belle Isle; the story now says so. (2) P. J. Colton's service runs at least to the 1907 keeper list (scan 146), not only to 1906. (3) 'wintered' changed to 'arrangements were made to winter' (LF's wording). (4) 1908 occulting-light reason is what the report links to the difficulty of transport; 'that season' was not in the source and is removed. (5) The 1990 heritage designation is cited to Lighthouse Friends only; the heritage character statement (CRHP 3905) does not give the date. Keeper tables: the 1902 table (scan 255, printed p. 144) was checked on the page image: the row reads 'Colton, P. J' with 'Belleisle'. The 1906 (scan 175) and 1907 (scan 146) entries were read from the OCR; the 1906 line appears as one OCR line ('Colton. P. J Belle Isle Light and Fog Alarm'), the 1907 name and station are in separate columns and were matched by row (4th name, 4th station), and the page image is not yet checked for them. Michael Colton's 1900 signature reads 'M ICHAEL COLTON, Lightkceper' on scan 117 (printed p. 20) in OCR; the image is not checked. Martin Colton and Martin Coltin are the same keeper only by LF's presentation. Scotsman: the wire and Dakota Chief items give 250 and 249 passengers; the Department's reports give no death toll; only one 1899 item gives fifteen drowned. Marine reports for 1906 (scan 52) and 1907 describe the North End station, which is a different station (built 1905); not used. Living-person rule: Clifford Flynn, Fred Osbourne, Abner Budgell and Fred Roberts are named only as Lighthouse Friends names them, with no personal detail. Not checked: Department reports for 1909-1924 for the fog alarm and radio station; the 'Lighthouse People' book cited by LF; Parks Canada's own page (did not render).
